blocks.text: In the first weeks after a severe spinal cord injury a patient's legs are limp and no reflexes can be elicited. Months later the same legs are stiff, jerk violently when tapped, and kick in spasms. The same cord, below the same lesion, has swung from one extreme to the other, which tells us that reflexes are shaped by control from above.

blocks.markdown:
A **reflex** is a rapid, stereotyped, involuntary response to a stimulus, mediated by a **reflex arc**: a **receptor**, an **afferent** (sensory) neurone, an **integration centre** in the cord or brainstem, an **efferent** (motor) neurone and an **effector** muscle. Reflexes maintain posture and muscle tone, protect against injury, and are used clinically to test the integrity of the arc and the influence of descending pathways.

**The monosynaptic stretch reflex.** The best-known example is the knee jerk. Stretching a muscle (tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps) excites **muscle spindles**, stretch receptors in the intrafusal fibres. The **Ia afferent** fibres enter the cord through the dorsal root, and synapse **directly** on **alpha motor neurones** to the same muscle in the ventral horn: **one synapse, therefore monosynaptic**. The motor neurone contracts the muscle, opposing the stretch. Collaterals of the Ia fibres also excite Ia **inhibitory interneurones**, which inhibit alpha motor neurones to the **antagonist** muscle (**reciprocal inhibition**), and so this component is disynaptic. **Gamma motor neurones** adjust spindle sensitivity during contraction so that the spindle keeps signalling length. Descending pathways influence reflex gain through the alpha and gamma motor neurones and interneurones.

rows: Monosynaptic to alpha motor neurone; disynaptic inhibition of antagonist
Relaxation of the muscle when tension is high
Polysynaptic; also crossed extension of the opposite limb

blocks.caption: Reflex latency: conduction time along afferent and efferent axons plus central delay (about 0.5-1 ms per synapse).

blocks.title: Tracing the knee jerk
blocks.prompt: Trace the knee jerk and estimate its latency if the afferent and efferent paths are each 0.5 m long, conduct at 50 m/s, and the single central synapse adds 0.8 ms.

steps.text: A tap on the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps and its spindles; Ia afferents fire, travelling in the femoral nerve to the dorsal root and the L3-L4 cord segments.
The Ia fibre synapses directly on alpha motor neurones to quadriceps, which fire and contract the muscle; antagonist hamstring motor neurones are inhibited via an interneurone.
Conduction time = (0.5 + 0.5) / 50 = 0.02 s = 20 ms; adding 0.8 ms gives 20.8 ms.

blocks.answer: The quadriceps contracts and the leg extends; the latency is about 21 ms.

blocks.markdown:
**Upper and lower motor neurone lesions.** **Upper motor neurones (UMNs)** are the cortical and brainstem neurones whose axons descend (corticospinal tract) to synapse on the alpha motor neurones. **Lower motor neurones (LMNs)** are the alpha motor neurones in the ventral horn (or cranial nerve nuclei) and their axons to muscle.

- An **LMN lesion** interrupts the final common pathway: **flaccid weakness, reduced tone (hypotonia), reduced or absent reflexes, marked muscle wasting and fasciculations**, with a flexor or absent plantar response.
- A **UMN lesion** removes descending inhibition on spinal circuits: **weakness in a pyramidal distribution (upper limb extensors, lower limb flexors), increased tone with spasticity, brisk reflexes, clonus, and an extensor plantar response (Babinski sign)**. Wasting is mild and late (from disuse). Spasticity is **velocity-dependent** and may show the 'clasp-knife' phenomenon. Early after an acute UMN lesion (**spinal shock**) the limbs may instead be flaccid and areflexic for days to weeks.

rows: Muscles supplied by the affected roots or nerves

blocks.markdown: **Reflex levels and localisation.** Each tendon reflex tests a particular spinal segment: **biceps C5-C6**, **supinator (brachioradialis) C5-C6**, **triceps C7-C8**, **knee L3-L4**, **ankle S1-S2** (S1 chiefly). A **reduced or absent reflex** points to an LMN or afferent lesion at that segment or root (for example a compressed root). **Exaggerated reflexes** at and below a certain level point to an UMN lesion above that level. A lesion within the cord may produce a **mixed picture**: LMN signs at the level of the lesion (damaged anterior horn or root) and UMN signs below it (damaged descending tracts).

blocks.title: Interpreting a reflex pattern
blocks.prompt: A patient has an absent right ankle jerk, weak plantarflexion and reduced sensation over the lateral foot. Knee jerks are normal. Where is the lesion and what type?

steps.text: The ankle jerk tests S1 (S1-S2). It is absent on one side: LMN or afferent lesion of that arc.
Plantarflexion weakness and lateral foot sensory loss fit an S1 root distribution; the knee jerk (L3-L4) is normal, so higher segments are intact.
Reflexes are reduced rather than brisk, so there is no UMN pattern.

blocks.answer: A right S1 root (LMN) lesion, for example from compression by a lumbosacral disc.

blocks.title: Level plus type
blocks.text: Absent reflex means a lower motor neurone or sensory root lesion at that level. Brisk reflex means an upper motor neurone lesion above that level. At a cord lesion expect both: absent at the level and brisk below.

points: A reflex arc has a receptor, afferent, integration centre, efferent and effector; the stretch reflex is monosynaptic (Ia afferent directly to alpha motor neurone) with reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist.
UMN lesions cause spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus and an extensor plantar response; LMN lesions cause flaccid weakness, hyporeflexia, wasting and fasciculations.
Tendon reflexes localise the segment: biceps C5-C6, triceps C7-C8, knee L3-L4, ankle S1-S2; absent reflex indicates a lesion of that arc, exaggerated reflex a lesion above.

questions.stem: Which afferent fibre type from the muscle spindle initiates the monosynaptic stretch reflex?

distractorRationale.b: Ib fibres arise from Golgi tendon organs.
distractorRationale.c: C fibres carry pain and temperature.
distractorRationale.d: Gamma efferents are motor fibres to the spindle.

questions.explanation: Ia fibres from the annulospiral endings of muscle spindles synapse directly on alpha motor neurones, producing the monosynaptic reflex.

questions.stem: What does the term monosynaptic mean in describing the stretch reflex?

options.text: There is a single synapse between the afferent neurone and the motor neurone
The reflex involves a single spinal segment only

questions.correctOptionText: There is a single synapse between the afferent neurone and the motor neurone

distractorRationale.a: The antagonist is also affected via an interneurone.
distractorRationale.c: The number of segments is not what the term means.
distractorRationale.d: Neurotransmitters are not the basis of the term.

questions.explanation: In the stretch reflex the Ia afferent synapses directly on the alpha motor neurone with no interneurone, which is why the response is the fastest of the reflexes.

questions.stem: When the quadriceps contracts during the knee jerk, the hamstring motor neurones are inhibited. What is this called?

options.text: Reciprocal inhibition via Ia inhibitory interneurones

questions.correctOptionText: Reciprocal inhibition via Ia inhibitory interneurones

distractorRationale.b: The inverse myotatic reflex is initiated by Golgi tendon organs.
distractorRationale.c: Crossed extension involves the opposite limb.
distractorRationale.d: The gamma loop regulates spindle sensitivity.

questions.explanation: Collaterals of Ia fibres excite inhibitory interneurones that suppress motor neurones of antagonist muscles. This allows the agonist to contract without opposition.

questions.stem: A stretch reflex is tested in the arm. The afferent and efferent axons are each 0.6 m long and conduct at 60 m/s. The single central synapse adds 1.0 ms. What is the total reflex latency in milliseconds?
questions.explanation: The total conduction distance is 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2 m, which at 60 m/s takes 1.2/60 = 0.020 s = 20 ms. Adding the 1.0 ms central delay gives 21 ms.

questions.stem: Which combination of findings is characteristic of an upper motor neurone lesion?

options.text: Spasticity, brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response
Marked early wasting and reduced tone
Reduced tone and flexor plantar response

questions.correctOptionText: Spasticity, brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response

distractorRationale.d: These do not describe a UMN lesion.

questions.explanation: Loss of descending inhibition in a UMN lesion increases tone, exaggerates tendon reflexes and produces an extensor plantar response.

questions.stem: True or false: fasciculations and marked early muscle wasting are typical of lower motor neurone lesions.
questions.explanation: Denervation of muscle by LMN damage produces fasciculations and rapid wasting, whereas UMN lesions cause only mild, late disuse atrophy.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has increased tone in the left leg that is greatest at the start of a rapid passive movement and then gives way, with a brisk knee jerk and sustained clonus at the ankle. Which lesion type does this indicate?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: clasp-knife spasticity, hyperreflexia and clonus are UMN signs.
distractorRationale.b: LMN lesions cause hypotonia and areflexia.
distractorRationale.c: Cerebellar lesions cause hypotonia and incoordination.
distractorRationale.d: Neuromuscular junction disorders do not cause spasticity.

questions.explanation: Velocity-dependent clasp-knife tone, brisk reflexes and clonus all result from loss of descending inhibition of spinal circuits, and so define an UMN lesion.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has weakness of elbow extension and wrist flexion, and an absent triceps jerk. Which spinal segments does the triceps reflex test?

distractorRationale.a: C5-C6 is the biceps and supinator reflex.

questions.explanation: The triceps reflex is mediated mainly by C7 with C8. An absent triceps jerk with weakness of its movements suggests an LMN lesion at those segments, such as a root compression.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has an absent right biceps jerk and wasting of the shoulder muscles, but brisk knee and ankle jerks, spastic legs and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Which localisation is best?

options.text: A lesion of the cervical cord at about C5-C6
A lesion of the lumbar roots

questions.correctOptionText: A lesion of the cervical cord at about C5-C6

distractorRationale.a: Correct: LMN signs at the level (biceps) and UMN signs below it (legs).
distractorRationale.b: Lumbar root lesions cause LMN signs in the legs, not spasticity.
distractorRationale.c: A neuropathy would not produce brisk reflexes and Babinski signs.
distractorRationale.d: Cerebellar lesions do not cause these tone and reflex changes.

questions.explanation: Absent biceps jerk with wasting indicates LMN damage at C5-C6, while the brisk lower limb reflexes, spasticity and extensor plantars indicate interrupted descending tracts below that level. The combination localises the lesion to the cord at that level.

questions.stem: Contrast upper and lower motor neurone lesions in terms of tone, reflexes, wasting, fasciculations and plantar response, and explain why reflexes are exaggerated after an UMN lesion.
markingGuide: UMN: increased tone (spasticity), brisk reflexes with clonus, extensor plantar, mild late wasting, no fasciculations
LMN: reduced tone, reduced or absent reflexes, marked wasting, fasciculations, flexor or absent plantar
UMN lesions remove descending inhibition of spinal reflex circuits (and the alpha and gamma motor neurones)
LMN lesions interrupt the final common pathway to the muscle
Spinal shock may cause initial flaccidity after an acute UMN lesion
questions.explanation: The corticospinal and other descending tracts normally restrain spinal reflexes. Without them, the stretch reflex gain is increased, producing spasticity and hyperreflexia, whereas an LMN lesion removes the efferent limb altogether.
